title: Review: Education and the Cult of Efficiency by Raymond E. Callahan
author: Lance Eaton
summary: Lance Eaton reviews Raymond Callahan's 1964 history of how Taylorist efficiency thinking took hold of American public school administration, and finds it uncomfortably current. Callahan shows superintendents becoming a professional class shaped by the discourse of efficiency, producing reports and numbers that demonstrated thrift without necessarily demonstrating learning. Eaton notes the real costs of that logic: larger classes, more demanded of poorly paid teachers, de-skilled work, and the loss of offerings such as Latin and Greek that did not fill classrooms. He connects the book to C. Thi Nguyen on value capture and to the political tension between public education as a shared good and rugged individualism. His sharpest turn is toward AI, which he fears gives efficiency-minded leaders a powerful new way to identify expensive skilled labor, break it into measurable pieces and replace it. He closes unconvinced that education has escaped the cult of efficiency, or even recognizes how deeply embedded it is.
points: Callahan traces how Taylorism and the professionalization of school administration made efficiency the dominant lens in public education for over a century.

Efficiency metrics can displace educational purpose, as when Latin and Greek disappeared because classes did not fill, so that full classes mattered more than full opportunity for intellectual pursuit.
Measurement becomes a trap when a proxy for learning comes to determine how schools operate, a problem of value capture.
Eaton warns that AI hands efficiency-minded administrators a tool to break skilled teaching into measurable parts and replace it, and treats Callahan's history as close to a playbook.
He predicts a gig-style class of on-call proctors as institutions respond to AI by returning to surveilled testing.
quotes: Callahan shows what can happen when efficiency becomes the easiest and therefore most important metric.
They found increasingly elaborate ways to produce reports and numbers that demonstrated efficiency without necessarily demonstrating actual learning.
The important thing becomes full classes rather than full opportunity for intellectual pursuit. That’s its own kind of harm because it quietly changes what we think education is supposed to be.
we measure something that represents another thing, a proxy for what we’re actually trying to get at, and eventually the measurement becomes a trap that determines how we go about doing things.
Reading it now feels like standing at another point along the same timeline and realizing that many of these problems haven’t changed. In some ways, they’ve gotten worse.
identify expensive skilled labor, break it into measurable pieces, find efficiencies, and demonstrate success through numbers. AI gives us an extraordinarily powerful new tool for doing exactly that.
More than a century after the story Callahan tells begins, I’m not convinced we’ve figured out how to escape the cult of efficiency.
